newsitem.title: USA: Westin ads asks "Who is he/she sleeping with?".
newsitem.headline: Westin ads asks "Who is he/she sleeping with?".

text.p: Westin Hotels & Resorts is looking to get noticed, and it's not afraid of using a little sexual wordplay to do the trick.

A global print advertising campaign for the Seattle-based hotel and resort chain breaking this month features milestone accomplishments of prominent Westin customers like former basketball star Isiah Thomas and other celebrities.
Each ad carries the suggestive tagline, "Who is he/she sleeping with?" and answers with the theme: "Choose your travel partner wisely."
The print campaign, by DDB Needham Chicago, is the second phase of Westin's $25 million brand-building ad campaign that broke in May on network, cable and local television worldwide.

"Traditional hotel advertising focuses on pretty lobbies, floral arrangements, handshakes," said Sue Brush, vice president-advertising and public relations for Westin. "We purposely wanted to so something diametrically opposed to that."
Westin's unconventional positioning was an effort to break through the clutter of advertising aimed at business travelers.

"We had to do something that was totally arresting. And the idea of relating it to sleep we thought was clever. We are in the business of selling sleep," Brush said, who referred to the double entendre in the question "Who is he/she sleeping with?" as the "fun part."
While most hotels catering to business travelers tout their amenities, convenience and services, Westin is selling a state of mind.

"Westin made it clear from the start that they wanted to distinguish themselves," said Judith Werme, group creative director at DDB Needham. "They wanted people to notice them. They wanted the kind of work we do for Anheuser-Busch," she said.
Westin's campaign takes aim at business travelers aged 24 to 44, shaving a decade from its previous target of 34- to 54-year-olds.
"With high technology, more and more mid-level managers are travelling for business. So we want to tap a new market," Brush said.
Westin's research showed that business travelers in this age group were driven by needs that reward their self-esteem.
"We wanted the ads to focus on this hard-driving, successful, aggressive business traveller," she said.

One of the print executions features a business card and photograph of Thomas, now the vice president/owner of the Toronto Raptors Basketball Club. The copy reads: "He got a real haircut with his first check. He bought a team with his last one. Who is he sleeping with? Westin. Choose your travel partner wisely."
Another ad spotlights Carmen Policy, president of the San Francisco Forty Niners. The copy says, "He has five Super Bowl rings. And he hasn't worn cleats since high school."

In the U.S., the campaign broke in September issues of Fortune, Newsweek Business Week, Conde Nast Traveller, Travel & Leisure and Family Life. Similar ads are running in Europe, Asia, Canada and Mexico.
The advertising push is part of Westin Chairman-Chief Executive Juergen Bartels' aggressive growth plan for the hotel chain. Analysts applaud the company's new spirit.

"Westin hasn't been all that prominent in putting itself before the public. This campaign reflects the new direction Westin is taking," said Andrew Olsen, an analyst with The Chambers Group, a Seattle-based hospitality consulting company.
In May 1995, a partnership comprised of Starwood Capital Group and Goldman Sachs & Co., Nomura Asset Capital Corp. and the Edward Thomas Companies, purchased Westin from Japanese owner Aoki Corp.

Bartels set out on an aggressive expansion strategy, opening more than one hotel a month. But he has also tried to boost profit by lowering costs and raising room rates. Despite the higher prices, Westin's vacancy rate has fallen. The chain, which operates 41,000 rooms in 22 countries, has combined revenues of $2.4 billion.

Early in reign, Bartels identified marketing as a major key to aiding the company's aggressive growth strategy, boosting the overall marketing budget 60 percent to $57 million in 1996 and ballooning the ad budget 300 percent to $25 million.

The increase made TV advertising a possibility for the first time, said Brush. Armed with a new ad budget, Westin conducted an agency review in which DDB Needham defeated Seattle incumbent Cole & Weber and Chiat/Day, New York. Westin's current campaign was created as part of Needham's pitch.
The print ads will run through this fall. Next year, Westin will launch regional sales promotions, again using the umbrella theme, "Choose your travel partner wisely."
